transcript.content: Hello, what brings you in today?

Well, I'm here because I've been having this issue with eating at night. It's like... once I start, I just can't stop. I'll be sitting there, almost watching myself do it, telling myself to quit, but my hands just keep reaching for more food. I just don't have any control over it once it starts.
After these episodes, do you do anything to compensate for the eating?

Yeah, I try to make up for it. After a bad eating night, I'll... well, I'll tell myself I need to balance it out by just skipping breakfast and lunch the next day. Or I'll go out for a walk and just keep going, walking miles past my usual route. I'll stay out there pushing myself, even when my knees are acting up and telling me I should really head home.
How many times per week do these episodes of eating with loss of control usually happen?

Well, for the last several months, I'd say most weeks have had at least one night where I eat like that. And then, you know, I spend the next day trying to make up for it... either by skipping meals, setting some strict rules about what I can eat, or taking one of those extra-long walks I mentioned.
How much does your weight or body shape affect how you judge yourself as a person?

A lot, honestly. It's... well, I used to judge a good day by whether I solved a tough design problem at work, or if I helped out at the theater. That was how I measured things. But lately, I just... I look at my stomach in the mirror, and it feels like the whole measure of who I am as a person is just whether I look controlled or if I look sloppy. It really dictates how I feel about myself now.

Inability to stop eating once the episode begins despite intending to stop

Imposing strict dietary rules to compensate

Self-worth is substantially influenced by perceived stomach appearance, body shape, and whether the patient appears controlled or sloppy
